extracted.intended_audience: students, philosophers, and practitioners of scientific method and inductive logic
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to observe, experiment, and infer causal laws in nature, including the roles and limits of pure observation and artificial experiment and the principal inductive methods (Method of Agreement and Method of Difference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Main business of Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To ascertain what consequents in nature are invariably connected with what antecedents, i.e., to determine the effect of every cause and the causes of all effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction aims to resolve the complex uniformities of nature into simpler uniformities so that individual facts can be predicted given requisite data (knowledge of preceding circumstances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical decomposition of phenomena (mental analysis first)
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of ascertaining causal laws is an analytical operation: resolve complex wholes into component elements by mental partition first, then effect separations in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mental partition is indispensable but insufficient; good observation requires seeing the component parts rather than merely perceiving wholes. Examples of bad observation include inattention, conflation of observation with imagination or inference, poor partitioning of components. Rules for observing are essentially rules of self-education (preparing the mind), not an 'Art of Observing' in the narrow technical sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate degree and minuteness of observation
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent and minuteness of observation and the degree of decomposition depend on the particular purpose in view; one need only subdivide facts until able to see what observations or experiments are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to decompose to unattainable ultimate units; carry subdivision as far as necessary to determine required further observation/experiment. Avoid being imprisoned by ordinary classifications — consider decompositions beyond everyday language when needed (example: chemical experiments do not note planetary positions because experience shows they're immaterial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Baconian rule: varying the circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine which antecedents are connected with which consequents we must 'vary the circumstances' — meet antecedents apart or observe consequents apart to see their invariant attendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational rule of physical inquiry: find instances where antecedents occur without others, or consequents occur with differing antecedents, to isolate causal connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation versus Experiment distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation consists in finding instances in nature; Experiment consists in artificially arranging circumstances to make or produce instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment extends observation by producing a greater number and the precise kind of variations needed, and by allowing the investigator to place the phenomenon 'among known circumstances' for isolation and further controlled variation. Example: isolating atmospheric gases to discover oxygen's role in respiration required artificial experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage of artificial experimentation (isolation & controlled variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When we can produce a phenomenon artificially we can introduce it into known circumstances, control concomitants, and introduce well-defined changes one by one to observe laws under many conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: electric machine, Leyden jar, voltaic battery enabling study of electric phenomena; chemists introducing substances, heat, pressure, electricity to test reactivity. Artificial experiments allow producing further variations and testing behavior under diverse circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations when phenomenon cannot be produced artificially
rubrics_metrics.description: If we cannot produce the phenomenon (e.g., human mind, social phenomena, many zoological cases), observation must be used and it becomes difficult or impossible to isolate antecedents precisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such sciences induction from direct experience is at a disadvantage and methods must be more deductive; many uniformities of co-existence or succession can be ascertained but causation often remains uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation alone can establish invariable succession or coexistence but not causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation without experiment can ascertain sequences and co-existences (invariable antecedence within experience) but cannot prove unconditional antecedence or causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove causation we must reverse the proof by producing the antecedent under known circumstances and seeing the consequent follow (i.e., add experimental evidence). Without such production the observed uniformity might be due to a common ulterior cause (example: day and night).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to confirm causation by production of antecedent
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying an invariable antecedent by observation, produce the antecedent artificially under known circumstances; if the effect follows, the induction is complete and the antecedent is established as the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reversal (producing A and observing a) converts observational evidence into demonstrative causal proof; examples include producing crystals by creating the putative antecedent conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement (FIRST CANON)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more instances of the phenomenon under investigation have only one circumstance in common, that sole common circumstance is the cause (or effect) of the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply by comparing instances in which the phenomenon occurs and noting the single common antecedent or consequent. Examples: combining an alkali and an oil under varied other circumstances always produces a soap (concluding the combination causes soap); crystallization associated with deposition from liquid state. Limitation: the invariable antecedent found may not be the unconditional cause unless verified experimentally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference (SECOND CANON)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an instance in which the phenomenon occurs and an instance in which it does not occur have every circumstance in common save one (the one occurring only in the former), that differing circumstance is the effect, or the cause, or an indispensable part of the cause, of the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method compares an instance A B C (with phenomenon) to B C (without), attributing the difference to A. It is the common logical basis for many everyday causal inferences (e.g., wound from gunshot causing death). It more strictly requires identical circumstances except for the one variable and is therefore especially suited to artificial experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods as elimination procedures and comparative suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Both Agreement and Difference are methods of elimination: successive exclusion of various accompanying circumstances to determine what is connected by law; the Method of Difference eliminates what can be absent only with loss of the phenomenon, the Method of Agreement eliminates what can be absent without prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method of Difference is more particularly a method of artificial experiment (requires precisely similar instances except for the variable introduced) while Method of Agreement is more adaptable to pure observation (any instances where the phenomenon occurs may be compared). Practical implication: when experiment is possible, Difference gives stronger assurance of causation; when only observation is possible, Agreement gives partial but still valuable invariable antecedents/consequents.
